title: Anchoring on Credit Spreads
research_question: Does a firm's prior borrowing cost influence the interest rate it receives on a subsequent loan, beyond what current fundamentals and market conditions justify? Specifically, do firms that last borrowed when credit spreads were high pay a premium, and those that last borrowed when spreads were low receive a discount, on new loans today, and if so, why?
data_description: The sample is drawn from the Reuters Dealscan database, covering term loans and long-term lines of credit (revolvers with maturity of at least one year) originated between 1987 and 2008. The unit of observation is an individual loan tranche. The sample is restricted to firms that borrow at least twice during the period, with at least one year between consecutive loans, yielding 15,536 loan-level observations (about one-quarter term loans, the rest long-term revolvers). A subset of 8,525 observations is matched to quarterly Compustat financials. Key loan-level variables include the all-in-drawn spread over LIBOR, loan amount, maturity, collateral, covenants, performance pricing, fees, lead arranger identity and market share, and loan purpose. Borrower variables include sales, assets, leverage, profitability (ROA), current ratio, market-to-book, stock returns, return volatility, and S&P long-term debt ratings (including unrated firms).
institutional_context: The setting is the U.S. syndicated loan market, a large and competitive market in which corporate borrowers negotiate loan pricing (spreads over LIBOR), fees, collateral, and covenants with a lead arranging bank that then forms a lending syndicate. Spreads should, in principle, reflect forward-looking assessments of default probability, recovery, illiquidity, and macro risk. However, repeat borrowing relationships are common: many firms return to debt markets multiple times, sometimes with the same lead arranger and sometimes switching, and aggregate credit conditions fluctuate substantially over the 1987–2008 period (e.g., the late-1990s tightening, post-tech-bubble loosening, and the 2008 financial crisis). This creates variation in the gap between aggregate spreads when a firm last borrowed and when it borrows again, and offers a setting to assess whether seemingly stale historical deal terms—particularly a firm's previously paid spread—influence current loan pricing despite competitive pressures.
